ospfVirtNbrEvents OBJECT-TYPE
SYNTAX Counter32
MAX-ACCESS read-only
STATUS current
DESCRIPTION
"The number of times this virtual link has
changed its state or an error has occurred.
Discontinuities in the value of this counter can occur
at re-initialization of the management system, and at other
times as indicated by the value of ospfDiscontinuityTime."
::= { ospfVirtNbrEntry 6 }

SYNTAX Counter32
MAX-ACCESS read-only
STATUS current
DESCRIPTION

Discontinuities in the value of this counter can occur
at re-initialization of the management system, and at other
times as indicated by the value of ospfDiscontinuityTime."
::= { ospfVirtNbrEntry 6 }

orig_text:
ospfTrapCompliance MODULE-COMPLIANCE
        STATUS       obsolete
        DESCRIPTION
           "The compliance statement."
        MODULE       -- this module
        MANDATORY-GROUPS { ospfTrapControlGroup }

        GROUP       ospfTrapControlGroup
        DESCRIPTION
           "This group is optional but recommended for all
           OSPF systems."
        ::= { ospfTrapCompliances 1 }
correct_text:
ospfTrapCompliance MODULE-COMPLIANCE
        STATUS       obsolete
        DESCRIPTION
           "The compliance statement."
        MODULE       -- this module
        GROUP       ospfTrapControlGroup
        DESCRIPTION
           "This group is optional but recommended for all
           OSPF systems."
        ::= { ospfTrapCompliances 1 }
notes:
ospfTrapControlGroup is listed both in the MANDATORY-GROUPS clause and in a GROUP clause. Per RFC 2580, Conformance Statements for SMIv2 (brackets added to indicate pertinent rule):

"5.4.2.  Mapping of the GROUP clause

   The GROUP clause, which need not be present, is repeatedly used to
   name each object and notification group which is conditionally
   mandatory for compliance to the MIB module.  The GROUP clause can
   also be used to name unconditionally optional groups.  [A group named
   in a GROUP clause must be absent from the correspondent MANDATORY-
   GROUPS clause.]"

It is listed in both clauses in RFC 1850 as well (which RFC 4750 obsoletes). It is STATUS current in RFC 1850 and STATUS obsolete in 4750; however, obsolete or not, it is not legal according to SMI rules.

orig_text:
The Neighbor Table and the Virtual Neighbor Table describe the
   neighbors to the OSPF Process.
correct_text:
The Neighbor Table and the Virtual Neighbor Table describe the
   neighbors to the OSPF Process. It should be noted that Neighbor table has a
   limitation. The index definition of ospfNbrTable does not guarantee unique
   identification of OSPF neighbor entries in a topology where multiple
   unnumbered interfaces on one router connect to numbered interfaces on another router.
notes:
1. Introduction

The index definition of ospfNbrTable does not guarantee unique identification of
OSPF neighbor entries in a topology where multiple unnumbered interfaces on one 
router connect to numbered interfaces on another router.

This can result in duplicate SNMP table indexes for distinct OSPF neighbor adjacencies.

2. Existing specification

RFC 4750 defines the index of ospfNbrEntry as:

INDEX { ospfNbrIpAddr, ospfNbrAddressLessIndex }

The specification defines ospfNbrAddressLessIndex as follows:

    On an interface having an IP address, its value is zero.
    On an addressless interface, its value is the corresponding ifIndex in the IF-MIB.

Additionally, ospfNbrIpAddr represents the IP source address used by the neighbor.
For addressless links, this is the address of another interface belonging to the neighbor.

3. Problem scenario

Consider the following topology:

                  Router R1
             (Two unnumbered interfaces)

                Gi0/0       Gi0/1
               ifIndex 10  ifIndex 11
                   |          |
                   |          |
                   |          |
               Gi0/0       Gi0/1
             10.1.1.2     10.1.2.2

                  Router R2
              (Numbered interfaces)

Assumptions:

    R1 has two unnumbered interfaces.
    R2 has two numbered interfaces.
    Both interfaces establish independent OSPF adjacencies.
    R1 uses the same IP source address for OSPF packets transmitted over both unnumbered interfaces.

Let the common source IP address used by R1 be X.X.X.X.

4. Resulting SNMP table entries on R2

Since R2's interfaces are numbered, RFC 4750 requires ospfNbrAddressLessIndex to be zero for both entries.

Consequently, the resulting neighbor table entries would be:
ospfNbrIpAddr	ospfNbrAddressLessIndex	ospfNbrRtrId
X.X.X.X           0                     1.1.1.1
X.X.X.X           0                     1.1.1.1

Both entries have the same composite index:

(X.X.X.X, 0)

However, they represent two distinct OSPF adjacencies established over two different physical interfaces.

This creates an SNMP table indexing collision.
